title: YOU CAN BE FORGIVEN AND STILL BE LIVING LIKE THE PERSON JESUS DIED TO SET FREE
paragraphs: YOU CAN BE FORGIVEN AND STILL BE LIVING LIKE THE PERSON JESUS DIED TO SET FREE
“If Anyone Is in Christ, He Is a New Creation” — The Terrifying, Beautiful Truth About What God Actually Changes When He Makes You New
There is a kind of heartbreak nobody talks about in church.
It happens when you genuinely believe Jesus died for your sins… but you still recognize the person you were before you met Him.
You still get angry over things you promised yourself you would surrender.
You still struggle with thoughts you thought prayer would have silenced by now.
You still carry memories that make you ashamed to look in the mirror.
Sometimes, you worship with your hands raised on Sunday, only to fight the same temptation on Monday.
And somewhere between another prayer for forgiveness and another night of disappointment, a question begins whispering inside your heart.
If Jesus really made me new… why do I still feel so much like the old me?
Maybe you have never said that question out loud.
Maybe you are afraid of what the answer might mean.
Because if you are honest, there are days when the promises of Scripture seem almost too beautiful to believe.
Especially this one.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
Read those words again.
Not might become new.
Not will become new after enough church attendance.
Not will become new when every temptation finally disappears.
He is a new creation.
Present tense.
A declaration.
An identity grounded in Jesus Christ.
But what does that actually mean?
Because if we misunderstand this verse, we can turn one of the most liberating promises in the Bible into another weapon of condemnation against ourselves.
And the tragedy is that some believers have spent years trying to become what God has already declared them to be in Christ.
There is something in the original Greek of this passage that deserves our attention.
Paul writes:
ὥστε εἴ τις ἐν Χριστῷ, καινὴ κτίσις· τὰ ἀρχαῖα παρῆλθεν, ἰδοὺ γέγονεν καινά.
Hōste ei tis en Christō, kainē ktisis; ta archaia parēlthen, idou gegonen kaina.
A close translation is:
“So then, if anyone is in Christ—new creation! The old things have passed away; look, new things have come.”
Notice something remarkable.
In the Greek, the expression kainē ktisis means “new creation.”
The word καινή (kainē) describes something new in quality or character. It is not merely a way of saying that something has recently appeared.
And κτίσις (ktisis) refers to creation or a created thing.
Paul is not describing a damaged person receiving a few cosmetic improvements.
He is announcing something far more profound.
In Christ, God has brought about a new reality.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because Christianity is not fundamentally a self-improvement program.
It is not Jesus helping the old you become a slightly more respectable version of yourself.
It is reconciliation with God through the death and resurrection of His Son, bringing you into a new life that you could never manufacture through human effort.
But before we celebrate that truth, we need to confront something uncomfortable.
You can change your behavior without ever surrendering your heart to Jesus.
You can stop drinking and still worship yourself.
You can abandon a destructive relationship and still live for the approval of people.
You can learn Christian vocabulary, memorize Bible verses, volunteer in ministry, and develop an impressive religious reputation while remaining spiritually unchanged.
You can look transformed to everyone around you while privately resisting the Lordship of Christ.
That is why the two most important words in 2 Corinthians 5:17 are not simply “new creation.”
They are “in Christ.”
Paul does not say that anyone who becomes religious is a new creation.
He does not say that anyone who joins a church, inherits Christian traditions, or learns how to behave around believers is a new creation.
He says anyone who is in Christ.
This is not merely a religious label.
It speaks of belonging to Jesus, being united with Him by faith, and sharing in the life and salvation that flow from Him.
And without that union, there is no new creation in the sense Paul is describing.
Jesus Himself made this painfully clear when He spoke to Nicodemus, a respected religious teacher who knew the Scriptures and understood religious discipline.
Jesus told him:
“Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” — John 3:3, KJV
Imagine the shock.
Here was a man who had spent his life studying the things of God.
Yet Jesus told him that religious knowledge was not enough.
He needed a new birth.
The Greek expression γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν (gennēthē anōthen) can communicate being born “from above,” while the word anōthen also carries the sense “again.”
John's account uses this meaningful expression to reveal that the new birth is not merely a human decision to start over.
It is a work of God.
Nicodemus thought about returning to his mother's womb.
Jesus was speaking about a birth accomplished by the Spirit.
And that is where so many of us misunderstand the Christian life.
We think God is waiting for us to become good enough to deserve transformation.
But the Gospel announces that we cannot save ourselves.
We need mercy.
We need grace.
We need the Holy Spirit.
We need Jesus.
Not as an accessory to an otherwise successful life.
Not as an emergency contact when everything collapses.
Not as someone whose name we mention while continuing to rule our own hearts.
We need Him as Savior and Lord.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes personal.
Because some of us did not come to Jesus with a respectable past.
Some came carrying scandals.
A broken marriage.
An addiction.
An affair.
A secret abortion.
A prison record.
A trail of dishonesty.
A history of violence.
A family we disappointed.
Children we neglected.
Promises we broke.
Words we can never take back.
And some came carrying wounds rather than scandals—betrayal, abandonment, abuse, and suffering inflicted by other people.
Not every wound is a sin you committed.
And not every painful consequence is proof that God is punishing you.
But whether you arrived burdened by guilt, wounded by another person's evil, or exhausted by years of trying to save yourself, the invitation of Jesus remains astonishing.
Come to Me.
Not because your history was harmless.
Not because your sins did not matter.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because His mercy is greater than anything you could earn.
Think about the apostle Paul.
Before he became one of the most influential witnesses to the resurrection of Jesus Christ, he persecuted the church.
He approved of Stephen's death.
He dragged believers into prison.
He believed he was defending God's honor while opposing the very Messiah God had sent.
And then Jesus confronted him on the road to Damascus.
The persecutor became a preacher.
The enemy of the church became a servant of Christ.
The man who once tried to silence the Gospel became willing to suffer for its proclamation.
But here is what makes Paul's testimony so powerful.
God did not rewrite the historical facts of Paul's past.
Stephen was still dead.
The families Paul had terrorized still had real memories.
The harm he had done was not imaginary.
Grace did not make evil good.
Grace made a guilty sinner a recipient of mercy and gave him a new life in Christ.
Paul would later write:
He remembered what he had been.
But his past no longer possessed the authority to define his standing before God.
That is the miracle.
Your history may explain some of your wounds, but it does not have the final authority to name you when you belong to Jesus Christ.
And perhaps someone reading this has been waiting years to hear that.
You are not beyond the reach of His mercy.
But please understand what that mercy actually cost.
God did not forgive sin by pretending it was insignificant.
The cross stands forever as the declaration that sin is so serious that reconciliation required the sacrifice of Jesus Christ.
The Son of God bore our sins.
He suffered.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
This is not merely an inspiring story about recovering from failure.
This is the Gospel.
Paul explains the foundation of our new identity just four verses after declaring us a new creation:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21, KJV
Jesus knew no sin.
Yet He bore our sin.
We had no righteousness sufficient to reconcile ourselves to God.
Yet through Christ, believers are brought into a right relationship with Him.
And this is why 2 Corinthians 5:17 must never be separated from its context.
Paul is speaking about Christ's death and resurrection, reconciliation with God, and the new life that follows.
In verse 18, he says:
“And all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ.”
The new creation is not a motivational slogan.
It is the fruit of God's saving work in Jesus.
But now comes the question that may be troubling you.
If I am new, why am I still struggling?
Why do I still feel tempted?
Why do I still have painful memories?
Why do I still get anxious?
Why do I still fight pride, jealousy, lust, bitterness, impatience, or fear?
Why do I sometimes feel spiritually exhausted?
Does that mean I was never really changed?
Not necessarily.
Because being made new in Christ does not mean becoming instantly incapable of sin, suffering, weakness, or temptation.
The Bible does not teach that every genuine Christian immediately becomes morally flawless.
In fact, the same apostle who proclaimed the new creation also wrote extensively about the believer's ongoing struggle against sin.
Galatians 5:17 describes the conflict between the flesh and the Spirit.
Romans 6 calls believers to refuse sin's dominion.
Colossians 3 commands Christians to put sinful practices to death.
Why would these commands exist if conversion automatically removed every struggle?
Because the Christian life involves both a decisive change in our relationship to Christ and an ongoing transformation into His likeness.
The theological word often used for this ongoing transformation is sanctification.
But you do not need a seminary degree to understand what that looks like.
It looks like a man who once justified his anger learning to confess it and seek forgiveness.
It looks like a woman who once found her identity in the approval of others learning that her worth is grounded in Christ.
It looks like someone who once hid their addiction finally bringing it into the light and seeking spiritual and practical help.
It looks like a father apologizing to his children without blaming them for his failures.
It looks like a believer choosing honesty even when dishonesty would be easier.
It looks like someone refusing revenge, not because the betrayal was harmless, but because they are learning to entrust justice to God.
Sometimes transformation is dramatic.
Sometimes it is painfully slow.
Sometimes there are setbacks, tears, accountability conversations, and difficult decisions.

And sometimes obedience feels less like standing triumphantly on a mountaintop and more like getting out of bed, opening your Bible, confessing yesterday's failure, and asking God for strength to walk faithfully today.
But do not confuse slow growth with the absence of God's work.
And do not confuse the presence of a struggle with permission to surrender to sin.
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 says that the grace of God teaches believers to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly lives.
That means grace is not merely pardon for the past.
It is also God's favor at work in transforming the present.
Yet we must be careful.
A person can become so focused on examining the evidence of their transformation that they stop looking to the One who saves them.
They spend every day asking:
Am I different enough?
Have I changed enough?
Have I prayed enough?
Have I repented perfectly enough?
And before long, their assurance rests on the strength of their latest performance rather than the sufficiency of Jesus Christ.
Friend, your obedience matters.
Repentance matters.
Holiness matters.
But your obedience is not the blood that purchased your salvation.
Jesus' blood is.
Your spiritual progress is not the foundation of your acceptance before God.
Christ is.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
And verse 10 immediately reminds us that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do you see the order?
We are not saved because we produce good works.
We are saved by grace through faith, and that grace brings forth a life increasingly shaped by obedience.
The fruit matters.
But the fruit is not the root.
Jesus is the source.
And when you understand that, repentance begins to look different.
It is no longer a desperate attempt to convince God to love someone He finds impossible to love.
It becomes the honest response of a person who has encountered His mercy and no longer wants to make peace with the sin that nailed their Savior to the cross.
There is another passage that reveals how deeply God has promised to change His people.
Long before Paul wrote to the Corinthians, God spoke through the prophet Ezekiel:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.” — Ezekiel 36:26, KJV
The Hebrew expression is:
לֵב חָדָשׁ (lev chadash)
A new heart.
And the promise continues with:
רוּחַ חֲדָשָׁה (ruach chadashah)
A new spirit.
In the biblical setting, the heart is not merely the center of human emotion.
It is associated with the inner person—desires, understanding, intentions, and will.
God was promising His people a profound inward renewal, not simply external religious reform.
In Ezekiel 36, this promise belongs to God's covenant purposes for Israel, including cleansing, restoration, and the gift of His Spirit.
Christians recognize the promised inward renewal as profoundly connected with the new-covenant blessings accomplished through Jesus Christ.
But we should not flatten Ezekiel's original context or pretend every detail of the prophecy is exhausted by an individual's conversion experience.
The central truth remains glorious.
God does not merely command His people to change.
He promises to work within them.
And this brings us to something that may change the way you read 2 Corinthians 5:17 forever.
When Paul says “new creation,” he is not speaking only about an individual's private spiritual improvement.
His words also point toward the greater reality of God's redemptive work.
The death and resurrection of Jesus mark the decisive beginning of the new creation.
The old age dominated by sin and death has been confronted by the risen Christ.
And those who belong to Him participate in the life of that coming renewal even now.
The fullness has not yet arrived.
Believers still suffer.
Bodies still age.
Creation still groans.
Death remains an enemy awaiting its final defeat.
But the resurrection of Jesus guarantees that the story is moving toward something far greater than a repaired version of the present world.
Revelation 21:5 records the declaration:
“Behold, I make all things new.”
Not merely better habits.
Not merely improved circumstances.
All things new.
The final restoration belongs to God.
And in Christ, the believer has already begun to taste the reality of that coming kingdom.
That is why the Christian hope is so much bigger than becoming a nicer person.
It is life in the crucified and risen Lord.
It is forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
Adoption into God's family.
The indwelling Holy Spirit.
A new allegiance.
A new hope.
And the promise of resurrection.
Yet perhaps the most emotional part of this truth is not what it tells us about our future.
It is what it means for the person who still cries over yesterday.
Think of Peter.
He promised Jesus that he would remain faithful even if everyone else fell away.
But when the pressure came, Peter denied knowing Him.
Three times.
The man who had walked on water with Jesus could not bring himself to acknowledge Jesus before those questioning him.
And then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61 says the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The eyes of Jesus.
The sound of the rooster.
The memory of his promise.
The weight of his failure.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
Not the exact circumstances.
But the unbearable moment when you realize you have become the person you swore you would never be.
When the excuses disappear.
When you stop blaming everybody else.
When you finally see your sin clearly.
Peter's tears did not erase his denial.
But his failure was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep, as recorded in John 21.
Notice what Jesus did not do.
He did not pretend Peter had never denied Him.
He did not teach that betrayal was harmless.
He brought Peter into a painful but gracious conversation about love, faithfulness, and responsibility.
And Peter's story continued.
Not because Peter had finally become strong enough to save himself.
But because Jesus had not abandoned him.
That is what grace does.
It does not deny the truth about your failure.
It meets you in the truth and calls you into a different future.
Somebody reading this has been living as though the worst thing they ever did was the truest thing about them.
You have confessed it.
You have prayed about it.
You have tried to make things right.
But every time you begin to experience peace, your mind replays the scene.
The conversation.
The betrayal.
The moment of compromise.
The look on someone's face.
The consequences you cannot reverse.
And the accusation returns.
You call yourself a Christian?
After what you did?
After what you thought?
After all the promises you broke?
But listen carefully.
If you belong to Jesus Christ, the final verdict over your standing before God is not issued by your shame.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
That does not mean Christians are beyond correction.
It does not mean repentance is optional.
It does not remove responsibility for the people we have harmed.
It does not mean every damaged relationship will be restored or every earthly consequence will disappear.
It means that those who are truly in Christ are no longer under God's condemning judgment.
Because Christ has borne their sin.
And that changes how we face the past.
You can acknowledge the wrong without making it your identity.
You can seek forgiveness without demanding that another person immediately trust you again.
You can accept consequences without believing that God has stopped being merciful.
You can pursue restitution where possible.
You can grieve what was lost.
And you can walk forward in obedience without pretending the road will always be easy.
A new creation is not a person without a past. It is a person whose future is no longer governed by the old life apart from Christ.
And now, perhaps, we need to talk about the person who looks spiritually healthy on the outside but is slowly dying inside.
You still attend church.
You still say “God is good.”
People still come to you for encouragement.
But privately, your prayer life has become mechanical.
Scripture feels distant.
Your conscience has been warning you about something you keep excusing.
Maybe you have been entertaining a relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe you have been hiding dishonesty behind financial pressure.
Maybe bitterness has become so familiar that you no longer recognize it as bitterness.
Maybe your faith has gradually become a public identity rather than a living relationship with the Lord.
And because people think you are spiritually strong, you are afraid to tell anyone you are struggling.
You do not want to disappoint them.
You do not want to lose their respect.
You do not want your reputation to collapse.
So you keep performing.
Smiling.
Posting.
Serving.
Singing.
While avoiding the very conversation with God that your soul desperately needs.
But what if the most important thing you do today is stop pretending?
Not announce every private struggle to the internet.
Not expose yourself to unsafe people.
Not confuse public confession with genuine repentance.
But come honestly before God.
And where appropriate, seek the help of a trustworthy, mature believer who can pray with you and hold you accountable.
Because secrecy can protect sin.
And isolation can deepen suffering.
James 5:16 encourages believers to confess their faults to one another and pray for one another.
There is healing in bringing what is hidden into the light with wisdom and humility.
You do not need to manufacture a dramatic testimony.
You need to tell the truth.
Perhaps your prayer tonight is simply:

Lord Jesus, I have been pretending that I am stronger than I am. I have defended things You are calling me to surrender. I have been more concerned about looking Christian than living faithfully before You. Forgive me. Search my heart. Teach me to walk in the new life You have given me.
That prayer may not sound impressive.
But the Christian life was never meant to be a performance for an audience.
It is a life lived before God.
And perhaps this is the point where the meaning of “new creation” finally begins to settle into your heart.
It does not mean that you will never cry again.
It does not mean that depression, grief, trauma, or physical illness automatically vanish at conversion.
It does not mean that every painful memory will disappear.
It does not mean that temptation becomes impossible.
It does not mean you will never need pastoral counsel, professional care, or the support of other believers.
It does not mean your life will suddenly become financially prosperous.
It does not mean that people you have hurt are obligated to reconcile with you immediately.
And it certainly does not mean that you become superior to people who have not yet believed.
It means that through Jesus Christ, God has brought you into a new relationship with Himself.
Your old life apart from Christ no longer has the same claim over you.
Your identity is now grounded in Him.
The Holy Spirit is at work within you.
And the life ahead of you is meant to be increasingly shaped by the One who saved you.
This is both a gift to receive and a calling to live.
Paul writes in Galatians 2:20:
Think about that.
The Christian life is not simply about asking, What would a better version of me do?
It is about asking, What does faithfulness to Jesus look like here?
When you are angry.
When nobody is watching.
When you have an opportunity to lie.
When someone insults you.
When temptation offers you a secret escape.
When you are tempted to give up on prayer.
When you are called to forgive.
When forgiveness does not mean restoring access to someone unsafe.
When doing what is right may cost you something.
When nobody applauds your obedience.
And when you fail, it means returning to the Lord in repentance rather than running away from Him in shame.
First John 1:9 reminds believers that God is faithful and just to forgive confessed sins and cleanse from unrighteousness.
That promise is not an invitation to treat sin casually.
It is an invitation to stop hiding.
Because the same Jesus who saves sinners also calls them to follow Him.
And His call is not comfortable.
“Let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.” — Luke 9:23, KJV
Daily.
Not once at an emotional altar call.
Not only when a worship song brings tears.
Not only when a sermon makes you feel convicted.
Daily.
In the ordinary moments.
In the decisions nobody sees.
In the battles that never become testimonies on social media.
In the quiet obedience that may never receive human recognition.
This is where new-creation life becomes visible.
Not in perfection.
But in a growing pattern of faith, repentance, love, and obedience.
And one day, perhaps without noticing exactly when it happened, you may realize that something has changed.
The insult that once would have made you explode now makes you stop and pray.
The temptation you once welcomed now grieves your heart.
The person you once hated has become someone you can sincerely ask God to bless, even if healthy boundaries remain necessary.
The Scripture you once ignored has become bread for your hungry soul.
The approval you once desperately chased has become less important than pleasing Christ.
You are not finished.
You are not flawless.
But you are not walking in the same direction you once were.
And when you stumble, you know where to turn.
Back to Jesus.
Not back to self-salvation.
Back to the cross.
Back to the mercy that first brought you home.
Not as a magical declaration.
Not as proof of salvation.
Not to impress strangers.
But as a simple testimony that you are looking to Jesus and trusting Him to continue His work in your life.
There is something deeply beautiful about believers reminding one another that the Christian journey was never meant to be walked alone.
And perhaps someone you know desperately needs this message.
Someone who believes their past has permanently disqualified them.
Someone who is confusing spiritual struggle with spiritual abandonment.
Someone who has become so religious that they have forgotten the wonder of grace.
Someone who thinks following Jesus means never admitting weakness.
Someone who has not yet surrendered their life to Christ.
Not merely to spread a post, but to make the truth of the Gospel accessible to someone who may never walk into a church or ask a pastor for help.
And if you have not yet placed your faith in Jesus Christ, please do not mistake reading this article for receiving the new life it describes.
The invitation is personal.
Turn from sin.
Trust in the crucified and risen Savior.
Come to Him with empty hands.
You do not purchase salvation through good behavior.
You do not inherit it through family tradition.
You do not earn it through religious performance.
You receive God's saving grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And faith is not merely agreeing that He exists.
It is trusting Him as the One who died for sinners and rose again, and following Him as Lord.
Perhaps the most important response you make today will not be something anyone else sees.
Perhaps it will be a quiet surrender before God.
Jesus, I need You.
I cannot cleanse my own heart.
I cannot undo my past.
I cannot save myself.
I believe You died for sinners and rose again.
I turn to You for mercy.
Forgive me. Teach me to follow You. Make my life a testimony of Your grace.
There is no special arrangement of words that makes salvation happen.
Our hope rests in Christ, not in the perfection of a prayer.
And for those who already belong to Him, the invitation remains the same.
Keep following.
Keep repenting.
Keep believing.
Keep growing.
Keep returning to the truth.
Because the new creation is not a trophy for spiritually impressive people.
It is a miracle of grace.
And this is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a personality around religion.
Not to sell the illusion that every Christian must look strong all the time.
But to keep pointing people to Jesus Christ through Scripture, biblical teaching, discipleship, encouragement, repentance, restoration, and the transforming power of the Gospel.

If these messages have helped you understand God's Word more deeply, consider following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, fellow believers, and even those still searching for truth to follow as well.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible, including to people who cannot afford to purchase resources.
And if you believe in this mission and have the financial ability to help sustain it, I want to invite you into something deeper.
For those who already practice generous giving, it can be a meaningful additional expression of Christian generosity.

Scripture teaches that supporting faithful Gospel ministry is honorable. Philippians 4:15–18 describes believers participating in Paul's ministry through generous gifts, and 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, not pressure or compulsion.
That distinction matters.
You do not need to pay Gospel Warrior to glorify God.
You can glorify Him through faith, obedience, generosity, prayer, service, and love.
These items are simply resources and expressions of appreciation. They are not spiritual rewards, and they cannot purchase a deeper relationship with God.
The greatest gift is still the Gospel itself.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Point someone toward Scripture.
Live the truth you have received.
Because the mission is not about making Gospel Warrior famous.
It is about making Jesus Christ known.
A Facebook share may reach someone who has quietly stopped praying.
A personal message may encourage someone who feels too ashamed to return to church.
A Scripture-filled conversation may help a friend reconsider what they believe about Jesus.
And a faithful supporter may help sustain the work that makes these resources available.
We cannot know what God will do with every act of service.
But we can be faithful with the opportunities He places before us.
And now, before you leave this article, I want to return to the question that brought us here.
If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.
What does that actually mean?
It means your salvation begins with God's grace, not your ability to reinvent yourself.
It means Jesus' death and resurrection are the foundation of your new life.
It means your old standing apart from Christ has been decisively changed.
It means your identity is now bound to the Savior who reconciled you to God.
It means the Holy Spirit is at work to transform your heart and conduct.
It means repentance becomes a way of life rather than an occasional religious performance.
It means your sins must be taken seriously, but they do not have the final word over those who are in Christ.
It means you can face the truth about your past without surrendering your future to it.
It means the Christian life is not sinless perfection in the present, but genuine new life that is being shaped by God's grace.
And it means that the resurrection of Jesus is the guarantee of a coming restoration far greater than anything this broken world can produce.
So the next time you look in the mirror and remember the person you used to be, do not pretend that person never existed.
Remember the mercy of God.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that the Lord who saved you is worthy of your obedience today.
And if you are still struggling, do not turn your struggle into an excuse to stop following Him.
Bring it into the light.
Seek help where you need it.
Confess what must be confessed.
Make right what you can.
Forgive where God calls you to forgive.
Accept that some wounds require time and wise care.
And keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because the most astonishing thing about the Gospel is not that God found perfect people and rewarded them with new lives.
It is that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
People with histories.
People with regrets.
People with broken promises.
People whose righteousness could never be enough.
People like Paul.
People like Peter.
People like you.
People like me.
And through His grace, He does what no human effort can accomplish.
He reconciles us to God.
He gives us new life.
He begins transforming us from within.
And He promises a future in which His redeeming work will be brought to completion.
So be honest with yourself one last time.
Are you trying to improve the old life while keeping Jesus at a distance?
Or have you truly entrusted yourself to Him?
And if you belong to Christ, are you learning to live in the reality of what He has done?
You do not need to answer those questions for an audience.
But you do need to take them seriously before God.
But above every invitation, remember the one that matters most.
Come to Jesus.
Not because you have finally become worthy.
But because He is the only Savior who can make you new.
The scars may remind you where you have been, but in Christ, they do not get to decide who you belong to.
